title: Navigating protein landscapes with a machine-learned transferable coarse-grained model
one_line: The authors train a machine-learned, transferable coarse-grained force field for proteins (CGSchNet-type) that reproduces folded structures, folding free-energy landscapes and dynamics across proteins it was not trained on.
key_claims: A single transferable coarse-grained model, learned from all-atom simulation data via force matching, generalises across multiple proteins rather than being fitted per-system.
The coarse-grained model recovers native folded structures and folding/unfolding free-energy landscapes for fast-folding proteins.
Coarse-graining plus the learned potential gives large speed-ups over all-atom molecular dynamics, allowing sampling of landscapes that are expensive at atomistic resolution.
The model is reported to transfer to proteins outside the training set, including capturing effects of mutations and disordered/partially folded states.
limitations: Performance depends on the quality and coverage of the all-atom reference simulations used for force matching; systems unlike the training set are less certain.
Coarse-grained representation discards side-chain and solvent detail, so atomistic-level mechanistic interpretation is limited.
Benchmarks emphasise small, fast-folding proteins; large multi-domain or complex assemblies are not established.
Coarse-grained dynamics are not directly comparable to physical timescales, complicating kinetic claims.
Specific numerical accuracy figures were not captured in the episode notes.
open_questions: Blind prospective tests on proteins and folds entirely absent from the training distribution, scored against experiment.
Whether the model reproduces experimentally measured folding thermodynamics and kinetics, not just all-atom reference data.
Extension to protein complexes, ligand binding and intrinsically disordered ensembles validated against NMR/SAXS observables.
